tytul: Elderflower jelly: why there is no recipe here
wstep: There is no recipe here for jelly made from elderflowers.

ostrzezenia.tekst: Herbs, flowers and infusions made from them are not naturally high-acid ingredients; to be canned, they need a tested recipe with an added amount of acid, sugar or both, even when the infusion is strained.

According to Ask Extension, the University of Wyoming pulled its recipe for canned dandelion jelly after a food scientist at the National Center for Home Food Preservation flagged it as potentially risky: the acidity is not low enough to prevent the growth of botulism spores, and the water activity may be high enough to allow microbial growth.

According to NDSU Extension, some flowers should not be eaten, so identify flowers correctly before eating them; flowers from a florist are meant to look at, not to eat, because some pesticides used on them have not been approved for edible plants.

akapity: According to Oregon State University Extension, an infusion made from flowers such as dandelions is likely not acidic enough to prevent the growth of pathogens.
That pulled recipe was for dandelion jelly, not elderflower jelly.
Elder leaves and stems contain higher levels of toxins than the flowers, so discard any stray pieces of leaf or stem.
Avoid making food from red elderberry (Sambucus racemosa), which may contain higher levels of toxins.
JarAtlas has found no tested recipe for elderflower jelly from a checked source.
